overview: What is genuinely new this period is the emergence of safe real-time autonomous planning as a large, fast-growing cluster, with multiple papers converging on online uncertainty handling, conformal safety guarantees, and fast-slow planning interfaces rather than pure end-to-end policy learning. The strongest acceleration remains in selective memory and perception efficiency: selective KV memory systems stay large even while stable, and coarse-to-fine multimodal reasoning shows the same idea moving into high-resolution vision-language inference. Long-horizon agent orchestration and dynamic reliability evaluation remain important but are no longer accelerating; the notable change is that their representative papers now sharpen the process-audit and evaluator-correlation problems rather than general agent capability. Mechanism-aware forecasting evaluation is still steady and conceptually important, but this week’s corpus suggests more emphasis on benchmark design and failure attribution than on immediate deployment pull. No previously dominant direction appears to have collapsed, though dynamic reliability evaluation is softening and looks closer to infrastructure hardening than frontier expansion.

macro_patterns.name: Selective perception under token budgets
macro_patterns.summary: The selective KV memory systems cluster and the coarse-to-fine multimodal reasoning cluster are converging on the same systems move: stop processing every token or pixel uniformly, and learn what to keep, quantize, crop, or revisit. Both are reacting to hard memory-bandwidth and latency ceilings in long-context and high-resolution inference, not just model-quality limits.
macro_patterns.so_what: Serving advantage shifts from raw model size to controllers that decide what not to read, because memory traffic becomes the dominant cost in both text and vision inference.

macro_patterns.name: Runtime trust replacing static eval
macro_patterns.summary: The dynamic reliability evaluation cluster and the long-horizon agent orchestration cluster both reject static benchmark scores as sufficient evidence of system quality. Research is moving toward executable, dynamic, process-level evaluation because long-horizon agents fail through correlated judges, hidden process corruption, and environment interaction that static task metrics miss.
macro_patterns.so_what: Enterprise adoption bottlenecks move from model capability to auditability: buyers need runtime evidence about process integrity and evaluator independence, not another benchmark win.

macro_patterns.name: Closed-loop uncertainty in autonomy
macro_patterns.summary: The safe real-time autonomous planning cluster and the mechanism-aware forecasting evaluation cluster both center uncertainty as a control variable rather than an after-the-fact confidence score. In both, the research shift is from passive prediction accuracy to mechanism-aware, intervention-aware models that can support real-time decisions under distribution shift and tail events.
macro_patterns.so_what: The defensible autonomy stack is no longer the one with the best average predictor; it is the one that can price tail risk online and show why its uncertainty estimate survives deployment shift.

clusters.label: Risk-calibrated real-time planning
clusters.one_line: Planning and control research is converging on online uncertainty-aware autonomy with explicit safety guarantees that remain computationally tractable in dynamic environments.
clusters.existing_landscape: Waymo, Cruise, Motional, NVIDIA DRIVE, Mobileye, and Applied Intuition all operate around safety-constrained autonomous planning and simulation, while ROS/MoveIt, Autoware, and MPC toolchains cover classical planning stacks for robotics. These systems already support prediction, planning, and safety validation, but most shipped products still separate offline validation from online control and lean on conservative buffers, scenario testing, or hand-designed uncertainty treatments. The common assumption is that safety envelopes are mostly precomputed, simulator-validated, or simple enough to fit real-time constraints.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The new work is not just better prediction; it is online adaptation of the safety set itself under interaction-driven distribution shift. Papers on online learning-based reachable set barriers, adversarially robust conformal prediction for interactive planning, and multistep belief-space dynamics learning all point to controllers that update uncertainty geometry during execution rather than treating it as fixed. None of the major autonomy platforms exposes this as a first-class deployed capability, because it collides with the real constraint: certifiable real-time latency under worst-case multi-agent coupling. That leaves a clear gap between research convergence on adaptive risk envelopes and industry stacks that still largely operationalize safety through conservative static margins and heavy offline validation.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is NEW and one of the fastest-growing in the corpus. The conformal prediction paper on interactive environments sharpens the issue by showing that policy changes can invalidate standard distribution-free guarantees, making static uncertainty calibration look structurally insufficient rather than merely suboptimal.
clusters.risks: Waymo, NVIDIA, Mobileye, or Applied Intuition could absorb much of this by extending their existing runtime safety and simulation stacks. The other risk is regulation: even if the methods work, certifiers may prefer simpler conservative systems over adaptive online uncertainty updates.

clusters.label: Adaptive KV memory control
clusters.one_line: LLM systems research is moving from fixed KV-cache heuristics toward learned, task-aware retention, quantization, and hybrid attention-memory architectures.
clusters.existing_landscape: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, Apple's on-device stacks, and cloud inference providers such as Fireworks and Together all optimize KV-cache handling through paging, batching, prefix caching, quantization, and attention kernels. Mistral-style sliding-window attention and hybrid architectures exist in model design, while production inference stacks mostly assume the model architecture is fixed and the serving layer applies generic cache policies. The shared assumption is that memory optimization should stay mostly heuristic, architecture-agnostic, and invisible to post-training adaptation.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The papers here converge on the idea that KV state is not just a buffer to compress; it is a learnable control surface. IndexMem learns eviction with latent memory, adaptive KV quantization allocates bits token-wise, and LightTransfer rewrites pretrained transformers into hybrid long-context models by identifying lazy layers and replacing full attention selectively. Shipping systems from vLLM or TensorRT-LLM do pieces of this, but they do not expose model-specific learned memory policies coupled to post-training adaptation, because that breaks the serving assumption that the runtime should not need to understand task semantics or alter the backbone. The hard constraint is memory bandwidth: once decode becomes bandwidth-bound, generic kernels commoditize and advantage moves to architectures and controllers that reduce bytes moved per useful token.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is only STABLE week over week, but it remains large and the representative papers have shifted from simple eviction heuristics toward learned memory controllers and lightweight architecture transfer. IndexMem and LightTransfer especially make the gap more concrete by showing that memory policy and model structure can be co-designed after pretraining rather than frozen.
clusters.risks: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, or model vendors themselves can add learned cache policies and hybrid-layer conversion over time. Confidence is tempered because this space is already crowded and strong incumbents sit directly on the bottleneck.

clusters.label: Process-level LLM reliability measurement
clusters.one_line: Evaluation research is shifting from static benchmark scoring toward dynamic, contamination-resistant, and dependence-aware measurement of LLM failure rates and judge quality.
clusters.existing_landscape: Scale AI, OpenAI Evals, Anthropic's evals work, LangSmith, Arize, Patronus AI, Galileo, Humanloop, and TruLens all cover slices of LLM evaluation, observability, and guardrail testing. They already support benchmark runs, rubric-based judging, red teaming, and some production monitoring, but most offerings still operationalize quality as task scores, traces, and judge outputs aggregated as if evaluators were independent and test sets were stable. The shared assumption is that enough benchmark breadth and workflow instrumentation approximates reliability.
clusters.research_industry_gap: This cluster attacks assumptions that many evaluation products quietly rely on: that unseen test sets stay uncontaminated, that multiple model judges provide independent evidence, and that failure rates can be estimated from biased auto-labelers with light calibration. LLMEval-Fair, the behavioral entanglement auditing paper, and constrained-MLE certification each expose a different structural hole in current eval stacks. No major vendor offers a reliability layer that explicitly models correlated judges and certifies failure rates under dynamic test generation, largely because doing so raises cost and weakens the marketing value of simple leaderboard-style outputs.
clusters.why_now: The cluster is softening in paper volume, but the conceptual gap has sharpened. The recent paper on statistical auditing of behavioral entanglement makes a previously hidden issue concrete: verifier ensembles can look diverse while sharing the same failure modes.
clusters.risks: This gap can close as a feature set inside existing eval platforms such as LangSmith, Patronus, or Arize. It is also a hard sell if buyers still reward surface-level benchmark movement over statistically defensible reliability estimates.

clusters.label: Stateful multi-agent orchestration
clusters.one_line: Agent research is converging on long-horizon systems that rely on explicit state continuity, role coordination, and process diagnostics rather than single-model prompting.
clusters.existing_landscape: OpenAI Codex CLI, Claude Code, Devin, OpenHands, SWE-agent, MetaGPT, CrewAI, and LangGraph already cover agent orchestration for software and knowledge work. They provide tool use, planning loops, memory, and multi-agent role structures, but most production systems still assume that better prompts, larger context windows, and generic traces are enough to sustain long tasks. The overlap is heavy, and nearly all of them treat collaboration quality as a workflow issue rather than a formally measured systems property.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The representative papers focus on failure modes that current products largely do not instrument: constraint loss across hops, competence miscalibration between agents, and the need for durable shared state with permission boundaries. AgentCollabBench and MetaCogAgent suggest that the missing capability is not another planner but process integrity measurement inside collaborative execution. Existing products expose logs and replay, but they do not generally surface whether an apparently successful output was produced through a corrupted reasoning chain or correlated overconfidence among agents. The non-research constraint is cost and latency: once long-horizon tasks run for hours, wasted steps and silent process corruption become an economic bottleneck, not just a quality issue.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is STABLE rather than accelerating, but the representative papers have become more diagnostic and less demo-driven. That shift matters because it reframes multi-agent performance as a runtime governance problem rather than a prompting problem.
clusters.risks: LangGraph, OpenHands, Anthropic, or OpenAI can add stronger state management and collaboration diagnostics without changing the core market structure. The space is also noisy, with many papers benchmarking orchestration choices that do not survive stronger base models.

clusters.label: Adaptive visual token acquisition
clusters.one_line: Multimodal reasoning work is converging on coarse-to-fine visual processing that acquires high-resolution evidence only where the task requires it.
clusters.existing_landscape: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Qwen, and LLaVA-family models already serve general VLMs, while NVIDIA and open-source projects optimize vision token compression and video pipelines. Products increasingly support image and video reasoning, but most still process visual inputs with fixed tokenization schemes or static compression ratios decided before task execution. The shared assumption is that visual encoding is a front-end preprocessing step, not an adaptive decision loop.
clusters.research_industry_gap: ERGO, AdaptVision, and related work treat visual token budget as a per-query allocation problem: first infer where evidence likely lives, then spend high-resolution compute selectively. That capability is largely absent from shipping VLM APIs, which still bill and run as if every image deserves roughly uniform attention. The hard constraint is inference cost and latency at high resolution or long video duration; once reasoning extends into the visual domain, fixed tokenization wastes compute on background and makes high-res understanding uneconomical at scale.
clusters.why_now: The cluster is STABLE, but the papers are increasingly explicit about adaptive acquisition rather than generic token reduction. ERGO especially sharpens the commercial significance by linking coarse preview passes to subsequent evidence-targeted reasoning.
clusters.risks: Model providers can fold adaptive cropping and hierarchical encoding into their serving stacks. Confidence stays medium because major VLM vendors already control both model and runtime, so they are well positioned to internalize the gain.
